/Issued 1258 PM MDT Mon Aug 17 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

A shortwave passage will maintain scattered shower and 
thunderstorm activity for the next couple of days. Similar to 
yesterday, ML CAPE levels will be running in the 500 to 1,000 J/kg
range with effective shear generally between 25 and 35 kts. 
Minimum RHs will continue to dip into the 20s, so brief wind 
strong wind gusts and cloud to ground lightning will be the 
primary hazards; however, there will be hail and brief heavy 
downpours with the stronger cores given the previously mentioned 
modestly elevated shear and PWATs around 0.75 inches. 

Ridging aloft strengthens over the Great Basin with heights 
rising as high as the 588 to 594 dm range over the Northern 
Rockies by Friday. This will reduce shower and storm coverage while
diurnal mixing maintains seasonably breezy conditions. Despite the
strength of this ridging, weak surface fronts look to keep
temperatures mostly in the 80s over central and north-central MT.
These features will have a harder time surpassing the central/SW
mountains, so upper 80s and even lower 90s are a safer bet down
there.

Subtle shortwaves will begin to move into western/southwestern MT
as early as Friday evening in advance of a trough moving onto the
Pacific NW coast. This wave will interact with diurnal 
instability and initiate isolated shower and thunderstorm 
activity, primarily over and near the higher terrain of W/SW MT 
with localized gusty winds and lightning being the most logical 
hazards.

The Pacific NW trough then approaches the Northern Rockies during
the weekend and brings increased shower and thunderstorm activity
and breezy to windy conditions. The main concern for this weekend
looks to be dry and continued very warm conditions and increasing
fire weather concerns. Southwesterly flow aloft looks to develop 
in the wake of the exiting trough early next week with passing 
shortwaves maintaining daily scattered shower and thunderstorm 
activity. - RCG 

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Mostly afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms through 
Tuesday night...

Scattered showers and thunderstorms will develop in a similar 
fashion as yesterday given the continued moist and modestly sheared 
environment. The one exception to this is the lack of a more defined 
forward moving surface front over the plains acting as a lifting 
mechanism. For this reason, storm coverage may be a bit more 
widespread over the southwest, but the more isolated central/north-
central MT storms are being highlighted with the better quality 
storm maintenance and upscale growth, especially as they cross the 
highway 87 corridor and the Little Belt Mountains. Should one of 
these storms gain momentum, then localized severe wind gusts and 
lightning will be the primary hazards followed by brief downpours 
and hail. Other areas will see similar hazards to monitor, although 
with less intensity in most cases given the mostly singular or weak 
multiple cellular storm structure. Peak timing for today's showers 
and storms will generally fall between 2 and 9 pm with coverage 
diminishing heading into the overnight hours. Tuesday looks to see a 
similar set up with scattered storms, mostly of the pulse variety 
with few isolated stronger storms capable of localized strong, wind 
gusts, brief downpours, and hail in addition to cloud to ground 
lightning. 

Elevated fire weather concerns this weekend...

A Pacific trough looks to bring breezy to windy conditions to the 
Northern Rockies this weekend despite increased shower and 
thunderstorm activity. Much of the forecast area has over a 50% 
chance for wind gusts exceeding 30 mph while minimum RHs fall to or 
near critically low levels. This is also reflected in the Hot Dry & 
Windy Index (HDWI) with probabilities for exceeding the 75th 
percentile on Saturday running above 50% for most locations. Recent 
rainfall has tamed the previously maxed out Energy Release 
Component (ERC) values and they are tentatively forecasted to 
remain shy of critical levels. If the mid-week warm up exceeds 
expectations, then elevated to critical fire weather conditions may 
develop for some areas. This situation will continue to be monitored 
for the need of fire weather products. - RCG
